INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
The National African American Gun Association
(“NAAGA”) is a nonprofit association founded in 2015
to defend the Second Amendment rights of members
of the African-American community.  NAAGA has
more than 40,000 members living in every state of the
United States and the Dist rict of Columbia.  Its
mission is to establish a fellowship by educating on the
rich legacy of gun ownership by African Americans,
offering training that supports safe gun use for selfdefense and sportsmanship, and advocating for the
inalienable right to se lf-defense for African
Americans.  NAAGA’s goal is to have every African
American introduced to firearm use for home
protection, competitive shooting, and outdoor
recreation, including with one of the most effective
firearms in America for those purposes: the AR-15.
The Asian Pacific American Gun Owners
Association (“APAGOA”) is a nonprofit association of
gun owners with an Asian Pacific American heritage
that is focused on promoting safe and responsible gun
ownership within the Asian Pacific American
community.  APAGOA provides educational materials
and other supportive resources to its members and
other interested parties, and advocates for strong
firearms safety, education, and community-building
initiatives.  APAGOA’s goal is to educate and empower

2

the Asian Pacific American gun-owner community so
that they can use their firearms, including AR-15s and
similar rifles, safely and responsibly.
The Liberal Gun Club (“LGC”) is an organization
of gun owners that seeks to provide a voice for gun
owners across the political spectrum in the national
conversation on gun rights, gun legislation, firearms
safety, and shooting sports.  With over 11,500
supporters and over 6,000 contributing members,
LGC serves as a national forum for all people,
irrespective of their beliefs, to discuss firearms
ownership and use and the enjoyment of firearmsrelated activities free from the destructive elements of
political extremism that dominate this subject on the
national scale.  LGC also actively develops and fosters
a variety of firearms-training programs and firearmssafety-education programs, including with respect to
AR-15s and similar rifles, for both gun owners and
non-gun owners alike.
Operation Blazing Sword–Pink Pistols (“OBSPP”)
comprises two organizations, Operation Blazing
Sword and Pink Pistols, which together advocate on
behalf of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and
queer firearm owners, with specific emphasis on selfdefense issues.  Operation Blazing Sword maintains a
network of over 2,000 volunteer firearm instructors in
nearly a thousand locations across all fifty states.
Pink Pistols, which was incorporated into Operation
Blazing Sword in 2018, is a shooting society that
honors gender and sexual diversity and advocates for
the responsible use of firearms for self-defense.
Membership is open to anyone, regardless of sexual

3

orientation or gender identity, who supports the rights
of LGBTQ firearm owners.
Amici have a clear interest in this case.  The
communities they represent are far more likely than
other Americans to become victims of firearms
violence.  And, unfortunately, Black, Asian, female,
and LGBT individuals are also far more likely to find
themselves in situations where they stand alone
facing groups of predators bent on violence against
them.  Amici’s members thus need the most effective
firearms they can get to defend themselves and their
loved ones—and can attest to the self-defense benefits
of the semiautomatic rifles that Connecticut and Cook
County have outlawed.  Semiautomatic rifles of the
sort these jurisdictions have banned “traditionally
have been widely accepted as lawful possessions,”
Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 612 (1994), for
good reason:  They are among the most reliable,
accurate, and easy to handle firearms ever made.  Far
from lending themselves to criminality, moreover, the
features that define the semiautomatic rifles
respondents have banned are what make them so
sought-after as self-defense tools.  Amici’s respective
members do not just want these reliable, accurate, and
easy to handle firearms; in  many cases, having them
(or not) is a matter of life or death.  Amici accordingly
submit this brief in support of petitioners.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Although respondents and their allies have
(mis)branded the firearms at issue in this case as
“assault weapons,” a far more appropriate moniker for
AR-15s and other similar semiautomatic rifles would

4

be “self-defense weapons.”  “Americans today possess
an estimated 20 to 30 million AR-15s,” Snope v.
Brown, 145 S.Ct. 1534, 1534 (2025) (Kavanaugh, J.,
respecting the denial of certiorari), for a reason:  The
specific features and firearm models Connecticut and
Cook County have banned are among the best-suited
for self-defense of any firearm currently available.  Far
from lending themselves to criminality, the features
that define the rifles respondents have chosen to
denigrate are precisely what make them so well-suited
to the Second Amendment’s ne plus ultra  purpose.
The ability to fire semiautomatically without the need
to rely on human muscle to rechamber a firearm and
the capacity to accept a detachable magazine are both
hallmarks of essentially all modern firearms because
they allow users to fire more accurate shots more
quickly.  And features like pistol and forward grips,
adjustable and thumbhole stocks, and barrel shrouds
and muzzle brakes likewise make handling and firing
easier and more accurate—not to mention more
achievable for the elderly, weaker individuals, and
Americans of all shapes, si zes, colors, and creeds.
Respondents’ flat bans on these safe, effective, and
reliable self-defense tools are not just inconsistent
with historical tradition, as petitioners have
explained.  They are also perverse, as they deprive the
people who face the greatest  need for effective selfdefense tools of some of the best such tools ever made.

5

ARGUMENT
I. Minority Groups Have A Particularly Strong
Interest In Ensuring That Citizens Can
Defend Themselves And Their Loved Ones.
For centuries now, minority groups of all kinds
have been the targets of violent crime in this country.
Racial minorities, for example, have throughout our
history (and even today) be en subject to lynchings,
racist attacks, and race-based gang and mob violence.
See generally Nicholas Johnson, Negroes and the Gun:
The Black Tradition of Arms (2014).  According to the
National Crime Victimization Survey, over 51% of all
reported hate crimes in 2024 were motivated by race,
see FBI, Uniform Crime Reporting Program, Reported
Crimes in the Nation  6 (2024), perma.cc/AN5P-ZE2J
(“Reported Crimes”), and Black and Asian Americans
face particularly high victimization rates, see Council
on Crim. Just., Violent Victimization is Decreasing—
But Not for Everyone  (Oct. 2024), perma.cc/U7V6-
T2XH; Aleisha Flores, FBI Hate Crime Data Reveals
Persistent Threats to Asian Americans Amid
Escalating Anti-I mmigrant Climate , Asian Ams.
Advancing Just. (Aug. 17, 2026), perma.cc/C7F4-
P6Z4.
Sexual minorities are likewise disproportionately
subject to violence based on  discriminatory animus.
Congress itself recognized as much when it enacted
the Matthew Shepard Hate Crimes Prevention Act of
2009, which expanded the scope of the federal statute
to include violence driven by a perpetrator’s animus
toward the victim’s actual or perceived sexual
orientation or gender identity.  18 U.S.C. §249(a)(2).
The FBI also reports that approximately one-fifth of

6

all hate crimes are motivated by such bias, which
makes this category of hate crime third only to crimes
based on race and religion.  See Reported Crimes ,
supra, at 6; see also Delphine Luneau, FBI’s Annual
Crime Report: Hate Crimes Against LGBTQ+
Community Remain Among Top 3 Most Reported
Categories, Human Rts. Campaign (Aug. 5, 2025),
perma.cc/5WXG-K7GV; LGBT people five times more
likely than non-LGBT people to be victims of violent
crime, Williams Inst., UCLA Sch. of Law (Feb. 13,
2025), perma.cc/N3JY-NHXY.
Despite the passage of the Violence Against
Women Act, Pub. L. No . 103-322, §40001, 108 Stat.
1796, 1902 (1994), cis-gender wo men, too, fall victim
to disproportionately high rates of violence today.
Women are often targets because of their perceived
vulnerability to male predators, whether in the form
of domestic violence by husbands and boyfriends or
street violence by common muggers and rapists.  See
Reported Crimes , supra, at 6-9; see also  FBI, FBI
Releases Domestic Violence Special Report  (Feb. 11,
2026), perma.cc/ERL3-FWHN (reporting that nearly
75% of domestic violence victims are women); Kelly
Jordan, Violence Against Women a Growing Concern ,
Emory Rollins Sch. of Pub.  Health (Mar. 5, 2025),
perma.cc/WTC9-48NS (finding that, on average, “one
woman is being murdered every 10 minutes by an
intimate partner or a family member”).
Given the particular dangers they face, racial and
sexual minorities must often be their own  first
responders, by arming them selves from the violent
perpetrators who would do them harm.  As civil rights
lawyer and criminologist Don B. Kates, Jr., said,

7

“Even if all 500,000 American police officers were
assigned to patrol, they could not protect 240 million
citizens from upwards of  10 million criminals who
enjoy the luxury of deciding when and where to
strike … [b]ut we have nothing like 500,000 patrol
officers” to patrol all communities, much less the lesspoliced minority communities.  Don B. Kates, Jr.,
Guns, Murders, and the Constitution: A Realistic
Assessment of Gun Control , Pac. Rsch. Inst. (Feb.
1990), perma.cc/5JDM-5VMV.  Law-abiding citizens
in minority populations of ten must provide for their
own protection, both at home and about.  See generally
Julie A. Ward et al., Reasons for Gun Ownership
Among Demographically Di verse New and Prior Gun
Owners, Am. J. of Prev. Med. (2024), perma.cc/4H2U-
2P3V.
That explains why an ever-increasing number of
amici’s own members and racial and sexual minorities
more broadly have chosen to equip themselves with an
AR-15 and similar semiautomatic rifles.  “Young
women,” for example, “are speaking out as to why AR-
15 weapons are their weapon of choice” in self-defense
situations.  See, e.g. , Lauren Fox, Do Women Prefer
AR-15 Rifles? , U.S. News & World Rep. (Jan. 30,
2013), perma.cc/B7MP-E5KC.  The same is true for
individuals in other minority and marginalized
groups.  See, e.g., Curtis Bunn, Why more Black people
are looking for safety in gun ownership , NBC News
(June 14, 2022), perma.cc/8E5M -N4DZ.  According to
a recent survey, 34% of Black individuals polled,
29.2% of Asians, 35.4% of Native Americans, 48.4% of
Pacific Islanders, and 38.3% of Hispanics owned one
or more AR-15 or similar semiautomatic rifle, and the
vast majority of those cited self-defense as the main

8

reason why.  See William English, 2021 National
Firearms Survey: Updated Analysis Including Types
of Firearms Owned , 20 (Georgetown Univ. Rsch.,
Paper No. 4109494, 2022), perma.cc/E8H9-N6RZ; see
also William English, 2026 National Firearms Survey:
Results from the Second Wave, Including Current
Ownership of AR-15 Style Rifles, Other “Assault
Weapons,” and Magazines that Hold More than 10
Rounds, 10, 37 (Georgetown Univ., Working Paper:
Aug. 2026), perma.cc/L535-DTQF; Peter Holley,
Fearing That State Leaders Want Them “Eradicated,”
Some Transgender Texans Embrace Firearms , Tex.
Monthly (Mar. 23, 2023), perma.cc/22FR-EEPL.
Countless real-life accounts demonstrate how such
individuals have protected themselves and their
families from untold violence by using or simply
brandishing the arms that Connecticut, Cook County,
and other states and localities have chosen to ban.
See, e.g., Protecting America from Assault Weapons:
Hearing before the H. Comm. on the Judiciary , 116th
Cong. 9 & n.32 (2019), perma.cc/S7ZR-HR4D
(statement of Amy E. Swearer).  One particularly
harrowing example involved “[a] pregnant … woman”
in Florida who, “armed with a semi-automatic rifle,
gunned down one of two home invaders who had
broken in and were pistol whipping her husband.”
David K. Li, Pregnant Florida Woman Uses AR-15 to
Fatally Shoot Armed Intruder , NBC News (Nov. 4,
2019), perma.cc/ZS4Y-D3FC.  Other examples of lawabiding citizens whose lives were saved because of
these self-defense tools abound.  See, e.g. , RIT
Students Accosted by Gunman in Their Home, ABC 13
(July 13, 2013), perma.cc/2TXF-WZ96 (noting that two
home invaders, one of them armed, fled after an

9

occupant brandished his AR-15); Natasha Ishak, The
True Stories Behind The ‘Rooftop Koreans’ Who Took
Up Arms During The L.A. Uprising , ATI (updated
June 11, 2025), perma.cc/5Q3Q-U9AB (describing how
“Korean store owners” armed themselves with
“semiautomatic rifle[s]” during the LA riots after they
were “abandoned by the LAPD”).
To be sure, not everyone might feel the need to
arm themselves with an AR-15 or similar rifle for selfdefense.  “For those … wh o work in marbled halls,
guarded constantly by a vigilant and dedicated police
force, the guarantees of the Second Amendment might
seem antiquated and superfluous.”  Peruta v.
California, 137 S.Ct. 1995, 1999 ( 2017) (Thomas, J.,
dissenting from denial of certiorari).  Regrettably, it is
easy for those already-protected members of society to
overlook the safety needs of vulnerable communities.
Facing daily threats of violence is a world few of them
will ever know and that most could not fathom.  But it
is one that sadly exists today for many people in many
parts of this country, as it has been for centuries.  See,
e.g., Ishak, supra.  In light of that reality, the
“Framers made a clear choice:  They reserved to all
Americans the right to bear arms for self-defense.”
Peruta, 137 S.Ct. at 1999-2000 (emphasis added).
Of course, amici do not ask that lawmakers and
jurists, among others, leave their often-protected
communities or do away with their security details or
systems to the extent they have them.  Rather, amici
ask only that they recognize that everyday Americans,
and especially otherwise vulnerable minorities in
urban and rural communities alike, should be afforded
the same protection throug h the reasonable exercise

10

of the Second Amendment right to self-defense that
the Founding generation promised to all Americans,
regardless of race, creed, or status.
II. AR-15s Are Popular For A Reason:  The
Features That Render A Firearm An
“Assault Weapon” Under Respondents’ Laws
Are Highly Useful For Civilian Self-Defense.
The popularity of semiautomatic rifles for selfdefense among amici’s members (and the rest of the
country) is unsurprising.  AR-15s and other similar
semiautomatic rifles are more reliable, easier to
handle, and more accurate  than handguns, making
them an even better fit for self-defense than the once
“quintessential self-defense weapon,” District of
Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570, 629 (2008).  See
Nicholas J. Johnson, et al., Firearms Law and the
Second Amendment 1997 (3d ed. 2021).  Bans like
Connecticut’s and Cook Count y’s thus seek to strip
amici’s members and others of vital self-defense tools.
In addition to banning a host of common rifles by
name, respondents’ laws ban any semiautomatic rifle
with the ability to accept a magazine that holds more
than ten rounds of ammunition if it has one or more of
the following features: a pistol grip; a protruding grip
that can be held by the non-trigger hand; a folding,
telescoping, or thumbhole stock; a barrel shroud; or a
muzzle brake or muzzle compensator.  Each of those
parts, much like the whole of the AR-15 and the other
semiautomatic rifles respondents outlaw, is highly
useful for civilian self-defense.2

2 Some of the information below is derived from the factual
record developed in Barnett v. Raoul, No. 3:23-cv-209 (S.D. Ill.),
on remand from the Seventh Circuit’s decision in Bevis v. City of

11

A. First, the ability to fire semiautomatically is
exceptionally useful for civilian self-defense.
The advent of semiautomatic firing was the great
innovation in modern firearms technology.  The
modern semiautomatic action was invented in the
1880s, and semiautomatic fi rearms first started
coming on the market in the 1890s.  David B. Kopel,
The History of Firearms Magazines and Magazine
Prohibitions, 78 Albany L. Rev. 849, 857-58 (2015).
Semiautomatic firearms are different from leveraction, bolt-action, or pump-action firearms, which
require human exertion to reload a new round into the
chamber.  With a semiautomatic firearm, by contrast,
“[e]ach time the gun is fi red, the semi-automatic
action uses part of the energy from firing the cartridge
to automatically eject the spent casing, recock the
firing mechanism, and load a new cartridge into the
firing chamber.”  Johnson, supra, at 1984.
“Because the use of recoil energy or diversion of
gases in the semi-automatic action significantly
reduces felt recoil, semi-automatics can be easier to
use by persons who do no t have great upper-body
strength” compared to lever-action, bolt-action,
breach-loading, or pump-action firearms that require

Naperville, 85 F.4th 1175 (7th Cir. 2023).  The parties in Barnett
not only engaged in extensive expert discovery, but conducted a
multi-day trial at which numerous self-defense and military
experts testified regarding the self-defense utility of AR-15s and
similar semiautomati c rifles, especially as compared to
machineguns.  That trial culminated in a decision enjoining
Illinois’ ban, which is nearly identical to Cook County’s ban.  756
F.Supp.3d 564 (S.D. Ill. 2024).  While the Seventh Circuit
reversed, it did not cast doubt on the trial record below.  180 F.4th
1035 (2026).

12

human energy to reload a new round into the chamber.
Id. at 1995; see also Trial.Tr.at.198:23-200:5, Barnett
v. Raoul , No. 3:23-cv-209 (S.D. Ill. Sept. 16, 2024),
Dkt.234 (discussing benefits of semiautomatic
firearms as “home defense”  weapons for those with
physical limitations).  “For all users, the reduced
recoil” that the semiautomatic action facilitates—
which is far less than any self-defense shotgun and
than most if not all handguns—“helps keep the muzzle
on target, increasing the accuracy of a second shot”—
which has “obvious self-defense utility.”  Johnson,
supra, at 1995-97.
B. Detachable magazines compound the utility of
semiautomatic rifles like the AR-15 and its many
cousins.  Ammunition feeding devices, or “magazines,”
are a critical functional component of modern
semiautomatic firearms.  Modern magazines are not
mere passive holders of ammunition.  They actively
feed ammunition into the firing chamber.  See
Johnson, supra, at 1994 (“Semi-automatic rifles store
and feed their ammunition from a magazine.”
(emphasis added)).  When a user pulls the trigger, the
round in the chamber fires, and the semiautomatic
action combines with the magazine to feed a new
round into the chamber, allowing the user to fire a
second (and third, etc.) sh ot without needing to exert
physical labor beyond the separate trigger pull
required for each follow-up shot.  See id. at 1984-85.
So, without a magazine feeding ammunition into the
firing chambers, a firearm cannot operate
semiautomatically at all.   S e e  A s s ’ n  o f  N . J .  R i f l e  &
Pistol Clubs, Inc. v. Att’y Gen. of N.J . (ANJRPC), 183
F.4th 211, 247 (3d Cir. 2026) (en banc).

“semiautomatic firearms that accept detachable
magazines are so well suited  for defense of self or
others as to render all other types of firearms obsolete
for that purpose.”  Little Rep., supra, ¶17.
That utility of being able to accurately fire followup shots does not dissipate (let alone disappear) after
the tenth shot.  Quite the opposite.  “When a firearm
being used for defense is out of ammunition, the
defender no longer has a functional firearm.” Kopel,
History of Firearms , supra, at 851.  So having more
rounds at the ready is a benefit for civilian selfdefense, while “limiting a rifle to a ten-round
capacity … handicaps the user in a self-defense
situation.”  Little Rep., supra, ¶18; see also Watt Rep.,
supra, ¶6 (“Every [self-defense] instructor and

Adjustable stocks. A “stock” is the part of a long
gun to which the barrel, action, and firing mechanism
are attached, and that allows the user to firmly brace
the firearm and more easily aim with stability.  “When
firing [a] rifle, the shooter braces its stock against the
shoulder of the same arm she uses to operate the
trigger.”  Johnson, supra, at 1970.
A “telescoping” stock is just an adjustable
shoulder stock, which allows a person to change the
length of his or her firearm to fit his or her stature.
Telescoping and other adjustable stocks help users
safely and effectively operate rifles.  See Kolbe v.
Hogan, 849 F.3d 114, 159 (4th Cir. 2017) (Traxler, J.,
dissenting) (explaining that a telescoping stock
“permits the operator to adjust the length of the stock
according to his or her physical size so that the rifle
can be held comfortably”).  This is not complicated:
Having a firearm that fits the user increases the user’s
ability to control the firearm, which in turn allows her
to wield it more effectively to defend herself.
“Everybody has different physiology,” so, “to control a
firearm, the distance or the pull length of the stock is
different for different people.”  Trial.Tr.at.444:12-18,
Barnett, Dkt.240; see also id. at 446:14-19 (“[F]it is
very, very important to the efficient and effective use
for a firearm, particularly for self-defense….”).  “This
is especially true for the population groups arguably
most in need of a firearm for self-defense, the disabled,
the small statured, the elderly, and the frail.”  Little
Rep., supra, ¶19(C); see also What’s the Best AR-15 for
Women, Bad Moon Armory (updated Aug. 18, 2025),
perma.cc/53EF-GRMS (noting that, for women in

18

particular, an adjustable st ock helps “fit” the firearm
to “their stature”).4
Thumbhole stocks.  A “thumbhole” stock, as its
name suggests, has a small hole drilled through the
grip area which allows the user of a firearm to place
the thumb of their firing hand into the stock of a rifle
behind the trigger guard, mimicking the ergonomics of
a pistol grip.  See Watt Rep., supra, ¶6.  Like pistol
grips themselves, thumbhole stocks can create a more
comfortable and stable gr ip for the user, which
provides for greater accuracy and decreases the risk of
dropping the firearm or firing stray shots in selfdefense or competition shooting scenarios.  See Little
Rep., supra, ¶19(A); Watt Rep., supra, ¶15.
Barrel shrouds.  A barrel shroud is a piece of
metal or other material built to fit around the barrel
of a firearm, which provides a safe place to put one’s
hand when bracing the firearm.  Johnson, supra, at
1968.  While some manufacturers’ barrel shrouds look
“aggressive” or “militaristic” to some, the self-defense
utility is obvious.  Without such a feature, users would
have to put their hands “directly … on the barrel,”
causing them to “burn” themselves—which would
undermine their ability to fire any, much less
accurate, follow-up shots.  Trial.Tr.at.261:23-262:1,
Barnett, Dkt.236.  And, for that reason, “[v]irtually
every semiautomatic rifle/carbine … in existence” has
some kind of barrel shroud (or a protruding grip to
